About: Frame Clock and Event Coordinates

Source

Lecture
5 — Spacetime
Simulation
1 — Frame clock and event time (guided inquiry)
Concept
Coordinate time is assigned to an event by the whole reference frame at once — it does not depend on the event's distance from any clock and does not wait for light to propagate.
Serves
Define events and reference frames in spacetime; appreciate the physical meaning of simultaneity; establishes the shared visual language (frame badge, single central clock, frame-coloured grid) reused by all later frame sims.
Inquiry
Why one clock per frame? · What time is stamped for an event at x = 10 when t = 0? · Should the sim wait for light? · Do two frames agree on an event's time?
Misconception
That the recorded time for a distant event should include the light-travel delay to the clock (encoded as prediction choice B).

Guided Inquiry

1 · Events and frames

Let’s start with the basic ingredient. An event is a single point of spacetime — one place and one moment, written (x, y) and t. Frame S is the blue lattice of rulers you see here, and it carries a clock reading t. Every event you place on the lattice gets tagged with its coordinates in S.

2 · The time of a distant event

Here’s a puzzle to warm up with. Frame S’s clock reads t = 0, and an event happens far out at x = 10 (the dashed ring), ten light-units from that clock. Predict first, then place it: what time coordinate do you think S gives the event?

Now go ahead and place the event inside the ring, and read the t in its tag.

3 · What supplies the reading

So here’s the puzzle. Only one clock is drawn, at the origin, yet the event ten units away was given t = 0 anyway. What do you think physically supplies that reading?

Try placing events at several different distances — you’ll see each one carries the clock reading of that moment, whatever x is.

4 · A second frame

Now let’s bring in a second frame. Frame S′ — the amber lattice — glides past at v = 0.40 c, carrying rulers and synchronised clocks of its own. An event is placed off the origin. What do you think — do S and S′ give it the same time?

Go ahead and place one event away from the origin, then compare the blue [S] tag with the amber [S′] tag.

5 · Simultaneous in which frame?

Now let’s put that to the test. All three events on the grid are given t = 0 in S — they’re simultaneous in S. Two sit at x = 3, and the third at x = 8. Which of them, if any, do you think share one t′ in S′?

Now read the amber t′ tag on each of the three events and see for yourself.

6 · The relativity of simultaneity

So here’s what you’ve just uncovered. Two events that share a time in S share one in S′ only if they share a position. That’s the relativity of simultaneity — and it comes from the frames synchronising their clocks differently, not from signal delay.

Frame S — rest frame (v = 0)
Frame S′ — moves at v relative to S
t = coordinate time in S · t′ = γ(t − vx) = coordinate time in S′
v = speed of S′ relative to S · γ = 1.091

Core claim
The event's S time tag uses the full transform t′ = γ(t − vx), which generally differs from the S′ central-clock reading t/γ at the same S-moment — that difference is the relativity of simultaneity. In Newtonian physics every frame stamps the same t; here, because the event has x ≠ 0, S and S′ disagree on its time coordinate.

The Physics

Frame, clock and event time · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A time coordinate is not the moment the news of an event reaches you; it is a label a frame gives the event. This sim places events on one frame's grid, then adds a second frame moving past it, so you can compare two sets of labels for the same event.

What you'll learn

  • What an event is, and what a frame adds to it.
  • How a frame decides the time of an event far from its origin clock.
  • How a second frame, moving at speed v, labels the same event, and the formulas that link the two sets of labels.
  • Which quantity both frames still agree on.
Frame S (blue) with its clock at the origin and an event further along x. Frame S′ (amber) glides past at speed v.

What's on screen

  • Blue grid: frame S, with x and y axes. A click on it places an event.
  • Amber grid: frame S′, drawn when you switch it on. It moves along +x at speed v and carries its own clock at its origin.
  • Event tags: each dot carries its label, E₁ (x, y, t) [S], plus an amber (x′, y′, t′) [S′] line when S′ is on.
  • Top-right clocks: the S clock, t [S], and, with S′ on, a line for S′ and its speed v.
See itFrame S alone, with its clock running. Watch for: the clock in the top-right corner counting up, t [S].

03

A frame is a lattice of clocks

  • An event is one point of spacetime: a place and a moment, here (x, y, t). It is something that happens, not an object.
  • A frame is a rule that gives events labels. Frame S is a lattice of rulers with a synchronised clock at every point. The sim draws only the clock at the origin; it stands in for all the others.
  • An event's time is the reading of the clock beside it, at the moment it happens. The tag E₁ (x, y, t) [S] is that label, nothing more.
Frame S at the sim's opening settings. The event is out at x = 10.
The same event gets different labels in different frames.
Key idea. Coordinates belong to a frame. The event itself does not change when you change frame.
See itOne event placed at (4, 2) on frame S. Watch for: the tag beside the dot, E₁ (x=4, y=2, t=0.00) [S].
04

The time S gives a distant event

The time comes from the clock beside the event, so x and y do not enter it.
  • An event at x = 10 gets the reading of the clock standing at x = 10. At the instant the origin clock reads 0, that is t = 0.
  • With c = 1, the flash takes 10 time-units to reach the origin, so the origin first learns of it at t = 10. That is when the news arrives. The frame subtracts transit time; it never adds it.
  • What you see is a picture built from light of different ages. What a frame reports is a map, with each event carrying its own label.
Spacetime diagram, c = 1: light runs at 45°. The event is at t = 0; t = 10 is when the origin finds out.
See itAn event placed at x = 10 while S's clock reads 0. Watch for: the tag reading t = 0.00 [S], not t = 10.
05

What S′ gives the same event

Frame S′ has its own rulers and its own synchronised clocks, moving at v along +x. It relabels events with the Lorentz transformation, which Lecture 10 derives; here it is the sim's rule.

The term −γvx is the whole difference at a shared S time.
v

These are the sim's own controls: the grid follows.

See itOne event at (6, 2), shown in both frames. Watch for: the amber t′ differing from the blue t.
See itRun both clocks with S′ drawn. Watch for: the S′ origin clock, t′, falling behind the S clock, t.
06

Simultaneity depends on the frame

  • Two events with the same S time have Δt = 0, so S′ gives them Δt′ = −γvΔx. The offset grows with the separation along x, not with distance from any clock.
  • Events simultaneous in S keep a common t′ only if they share x (or v = 0). The y values do not matter, since t′ has no y in it.
  • The cause is that S and S′ synchronise their clocks differently. It is not signal delay.
Two events with one S time, labelled by both frames at v = 0.40.

If the clocks are running when you place events, all of them share whatever t the S clock shows. Every t′ moves up by γt together, so the differences are unchanged.

See itThree events with one S time: two at x = 3, one at x = 10, S′ on. Watch for: the two x = 3 tags sharing one t′, and the x = 10 tag reading lower.
07

The interval is the same in both frames

The two frames disagree on each label, but the relabelling keeps one combination fixed. For a pair of events, with c = 1:

Sign convention of Lecture 5: ΔS² is positive for a pair like this one, where space beats time. Here Δy = 0, so it drops out.
  • Take events at x = 3 and x = 10 with the same S time and the same y. In S: Δx = 7, Δt = 0, so ΔS² = 49.
  • In S′ at v = 0.40: Δx′ = 7.64 and Δt′ = −3.06, so 7.64² − 3.06² ≈ 49.
  • The sim does not print ΔS². You can work it out from the tags.
Key idea. The labels belong to the frame. The interval belongs to the pair of events.
See itTwo events at x = 3 and x = 10, same y and same S time, with S′ on. Watch for: Δx′ coming out larger than 7 and Δt′ no longer zero, while Δx′² − Δt′² stays 49.
08

Where it matters

  • Astronomy. Light from SN 1987A reached Earth in February 1987. The Large Magellanic Cloud is about 168,000 light-years away, so in the Galaxy's frame the star exploded roughly 168,000 years before. Astronomers subtract the transit time, just as frame S does.
  • GPS. Each satellite broadcasts the time it sent its signal. The receiver subtracts that from its own clock reading. The difference, about 67 ms for a satellite about 20,000 km away, times c, gives the range.
  • Setting clocks. Einstein's method: send a pulse from A at t₁ (A's clock), reflect it at B, receive it back at t₂. If light takes equal time each way, B's clock read (t₁ + t₂)/2 at the reflection. The delay is subtracted by construction.
09

Summary

In one line. An event's time is the reading of the clock beside it in a given frame. Another frame moving at v labels it t′ = γ(t − vx), and the interval is the same in both.

Key points

  • A frame is rulers plus a synchronised clock at every point; distance never enters t.
  • S′ labels events with t′ = γ(t − vx), x′ = γ(x − vt), y′ = y.
  • The −γvx term splits S's single "now" by position: Δt′ = −γvΔx.
  • ΔS² = Δx² + Δy² − Δt² is the same in both frames.

Common mix-ups

  • "The recorded time should include the light-travel delay." That is when the flash arrives. The frame subtracts it, so the event keeps t = 0.
  • "One clock at the origin does the timing." A frame has a synchronised clock at every point.
  • "S′ gives the event t/γ." t/γ is the reading of the S′ clock at x′ = 0. An event at x ≠ 0 gets t′ = γ(t − vx).

Things to try on your own

  • Turn on Frame S′, press Measure simultaneous events, and drag v from 0 up to 0.90. Read the three t′ tags at each setting.
  • Place two events at the same x but different y, then compare their t′ tags.
  • With Δy = 0, compute Δx′² − Δt′² from two tags at three values of v.
